paras: The killing of Noah Anderson was the fatal shooting of a farmer near Carlisle, Kentucky, by masked men who forced the door of his home on the night of January 18, 1881. Anderson died almost at once, and his fifteen-year-old son Samuel, who went to his aid, was reported killed by the wire and fatally wounded by a Carlisle correspondent. The wire story, copied widely within days, said the men had come to punish Anderson for mistreating his wife.

Anderson had farmed for seventeen years from a small log and frame house on the Maysville Branch of the Kentucky Central Railroad, about a mile and a half east of Carlisle. The Kentucky Gazette gave his age as sixty-eight and said he left a wife and ten children. A later paragraph described him as a cripple who "frequently whipped his wife," adding that his neighbors "were not inclined to excuse him."

About half past ten that night, six or seven masked riders called at the nearby house of Robert Anderson, Noah's married son, who said they demanded money he had of his father and left with threats. At Noah Anderson's they called him out and, refused entry, forced the door. Anderson stood near it with pistols in his hands; the Carlisle correspondent wrote that no one knew who fired first, while the wire said Anderson fired and the men answered.

Five or six shots followed, and Anderson fell with a pistol ball through his chest and died almost instantly. Samuel, who had been asleep in the room with a younger brother, caught his father and was struck by a .38-caliber ball while holding him up. According to the Gazette, the ball was taken out near his spine and his recovery was thought almost hopeless.

Early dispatches said no arrests had been made but that a man named Berry in Carlisle, who had a bad neck wound, was suspected. The Carlisle letter named him as George Berry, found nearby with a pistol wound in the neck, and said he was reported to have admitted being at the house. Anderson was buried the next evening amid what the correspondent called great excitement. Summaries in early February still called the mob's members unknown, and the coverage shows no inquest, trial or later word of Samuel.

Most papers took the story from a Cincinnati Gazette special dated January 19, which the Memphis Daily Appeal printed the next day and papers from Lancaster to Phoenix copied or cut down. Headlines ranged from "Fatal Shooting Affray" and "Killed by Masked Men" to the Wheeling Register's "Dastardly Murder." The wire gave the band's own purpose, to punish Anderson "for maltreatment of his wife," as the explanation, and the Delaware State Journal set the phrase in quotation marks.

Weekly summaries carried the story into February, and the Litchfield Enquirer reduced it to one line saying a father and son "were murdered in Kentucky, last week, by masked men." Other briefs recast it: the Weekly Elko Independent wrote that the men had attempted Anderson's arrest, and "A Pluckey Cripple" in the New York Sun and Sedalia Weekly Bazoo dwelt on his cruelty and his stand at the door. No paper stated the Andersons' race, though several printed the item beside the lynching of two men described as "negroes" at Prosperity, South Carolina, the same night.

Wire reports said Samuel was shot through the heart, or in one summary the head, and instantly killed, while the Carlisle letter and the Highland Weekly News described a fatal wound he had not yet died of. The local letter, which described the wounds within a day, is the closer evidence on his condition.

That letter also reported that Robert Anderson had drawn $317 of his father's money and that the mob was supposed to have gone to recover it for the father, though it called a theory of robbery untenable. The "Pluckey Cripple" paragraph said Anderson wounded the band's leader, whereas the wire named the wounded suspect only as Berry.
The Carlisle letter, dated January 20, placed the killing "last night," but the Cincinnati dispatch of January 19 already reported it, so the night of the 18th is the better-supported date.

bases: A band of six or seven masked riders went at night to a farmer's home to punish him for mistreating his wife, broke in and shot him and his son (A1, A4, A20).

Noah Anderson was shot dead by a masked band of six or seven acting without authority to punish alleged wife-beating (A1, A4, A20); it is 'probable' rather than certain because the band reportedly came to whip him and the killing came in an exchange of fire after he met them armed, and the local letter also raises a money motive (A4, A10, A21).
The Cincinnati Gazette wire and an independent Carlisle letter agree that masked men forced Anderson's door at night and shot him and his son (A1, A4, A10).

The Wheeling Register headed the Carlisle letter 'Dastardly Murder' and the Litchfield Enquirer said father and son 'were murdered'.
'A Pluckey Cripple' stressed Anderson's cruelty to his wife and his neighbors' refusal to excuse him while praising his resolute stand.
